clue.text: Where he sits to form his opinions might be easy, as well.

definitions.text: Where he sits to form his opinions might be easy, as well.

parts.words: Where he sits to form his opinions might be easy, as well.
parts.note: the seat he judges from is an easy chair, and the judging itself might be easy too, since he never has to act

explanation.walkthrough: The first word is the seat (an easy chair), the second is the person who sits in it passing judgement. 'Easy' works on both: the chair and the opinions.
explanation.definitionFit: An armchair critic is someone who passes judgement on things without practical experience of them.

clue.text: Her character emphasized the little grey cells.

definitions.text: Her character emphasized the little grey cells.

parts.words: Her character emphasized the little grey cells.
parts.note: Hercule Poirot, the detective she created, constantly praises his 'little grey cells'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' looks like her personality, but it is the fictional detective she wrote, Hercule Poirot.
explanation.definitionFit: The British crime novelist created Hercule Poirot, whose catchphrase about his brain's 'little grey cells' is famous.

clue.text: You might find one in a Chinese restaurant, though you might not want to meet one sailing.

definitions.text: You might find one in a Chinese restaurant, though you might not want to meet one sailing.

parts.words: You might find one in a Chinese restaurant, though you might not want to meet one sailing.
parts.note: read without the hyphen; with it, a dangerous fish at sea

explanation.walkthrough: Take out the hyphen and it is a diner eating shark's fin soup in a Chinese restaurant; keep it and it is the dangerous fish a sailor would avoid.
explanation.definitionFit: A man-eating shark is one that attacks people, the kind no swimmer or sailor wants to encounter.

clue.text: The diary he composed might typify somewhat dated entertainment.

indicators.note: composed means put together or arranged, so these letters are set out afresh

explanation.surface: A diarist's journal turns out to be a period piece about old-fashioned amusements.
explanation.walkthrough: 'composed' looks like the man writing his diary, but it rearranges the seven letters of DIARY HE.
explanation.definitionFit: A hayride, a jaunt in a cart full of hay, is a rustic outing that now seems quaint and old-fashioned.

clue.text: Such things can be seen to prove understanding.

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read as two words: things you can see
second meaning: deep understanding or perception

explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer in two and it describes things within view; as one word it is understanding.
explanation.definitionFit: Insight is a clear, deep perception of a situation, a kind of comprehension.

clue.text: See 1
Said to be placed in the woodwind, perhaps.

indicators.note: in tells us the placed word goes inside the woodwind word

parts.note: a reed is the vibrating part of a woodwind instrument, and stands for one here
placed means put

explanation.surface: Something is supposedly set down among the instruments of the wind section.
explanation.definitionFit: A person reputed to be rich is generally said or believed to be so.

clue.text: You're on solid ground here.

parts.note: the Latin phrase for dry land, used of being safe and secure off the water

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is Latin for firm land, and is used figuratively of feeling secure.
explanation.definitionFit: Terra firma is dry land as opposed to sea or air, literally firm earth in Latin.

clue.text: Possibly a plier as it once appeared.

indicators.note: the letters of 'as it once' appeared, that is turned up in a new form, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Something that might be a pair of pliers, as it used to look in the old days.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plier' looks like the tool, but it means one who plies: a canoeist plies a paddle. 'appeared' says the letters of AS IT ONCE turn up rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A canoeist plies, works steadily at, a paddle, so is an example of one who plies.

clue.text: Henry V suggested going into it once more.

definitions.text: Henry V suggested going into it once more.

parts.words: Henry V suggested going into it once more.
parts.note: Shakespeare's king urges his troops at the siege of Harfleur to attack the gap in the town wall once more

explanation.walkthrough: The clue quotes Shakespeare: King Henry's speech at the siege of Harfleur begins 'Once more unto the breach'.
explanation.definitionFit: A breach is a gap broken in a fortification's wall, which the troops are urged to storm again.

clue.text: A man no youngster has to bother, obviously.

indicators.note: has means the words hold the answer, so look for it inside them

parts.note: the letters run across the end of man, all of no and the start of youngster

explanation.surface: A childless man presumably has nobody small to pester him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' means the words hold the answer: it runs across 'man no youngster'. 'obviously' adds that it is in plain view, while the surface suggests a man with no children.
explanation.definitionFit: To annoy someone is to irritate or pester them, a close synonym of bothering them.

clue.text: You'll have to fight to press for the business some dealers are in.

definitions.text: the business some dealers are in

parts.note: a scrap is a fight
to iron clothes is to press them

explanation.surface: A warning that anyone pushing for this trade will have a battle on their hands.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrap iron is discarded metal bought and sold for recycling, a trade carried on by scrap merchants.

clue.text: Going for the title, perhaps?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: ... for a place is going towards it
second meaning: a title, such as one at the top of a chapter

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a contender chasing a championship; the two halves are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb form it means moving towards somewhere; as a noun it is the caption at the top of a page or section.

clue.text: Put into operation at acute trouble.

indicators.note: trouble here means disturbance, so the letters of 'at acute' are stirred up

explanation.surface: Measures are brought in at a moment of serious crisis.
explanation.definitionFit: To actuate a machine or device is to set it working or bring it into action.

clue.text: Straightforward conduct.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: frank and to the point
second meaning: to conduct or manage

explanation.walkthrough: 'conduct' reads as a noun meaning behaviour, but it is the verb meaning to lead or manage.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an adjective for frank, plain dealing and a verb for guiding or managing something.

clue.text: Some signals might be called after them.

definitions.text: Some signals might be called after them.

parts.words: Some signals might be called after them.
parts.note: in American football the quarterback calls the play signals once the team has gathered in a close group

explanation.walkthrough: 'called after them' looks like naming something in someone's honour, but it means calling plays once the team has gathered round.
explanation.definitionFit: Huddles are the tight player groupings in American football where the next play is announced.

clue.text: With the umbrella, under Edwardian rules it should show what could be cleaned up.

indicators.note: read as a rule that the words must show the answer, so it is visible inside the words just before

parts.note: the letters run from the end of umbrella, through all of under, into the start of Edwardian

explanation.surface: Etiquette for an Edwardian gentleman with his umbrella, and what he ought to display.
explanation.walkthrough: The talk of Edwardian dress rules makes it look like a riddle about manners, but 'rules it should show' points to the answer sitting in plain view across 'umbrella, under Edwardian'.
explanation.definitionFit: Laundered means washed, so clothing or linen that could be cleaned up is described this way once it has been.

clue.text: See 1 down
If the pigskin gets dirty, do they use this, or would that be nonsense?

definitions.text: If the pigskin gets dirty, do they use this
definitions.meaning: first meaning, read as two words: a wash for a hog, since 'pigskin' is taken literally

explanation.walkthrough: In the USA a pigskin is a football, but here it is taken literally as a pig's hide, which would need a hog wash.
explanation.definitionFit: Hogwash originally meant kitchen swill fed to pigs, and came to mean worthless talk or rubbish.

clue.text: Flower arranging lays the total amount.

indicators.note: arranging sets the letters of 'lays' in a new order, as in a flower arrangement

parts.note: the sum is the total amount

explanation.surface: A flower arranger tallies up how much has been laid out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arranging' looks like part of 'Flower arranging', but it works on 'lays' to give ALYS.
explanation.definitionFit: Alyssum is a low-growing garden plant with small white or purple blooms.

clue.text: Observed he precedes a misdeed?

indicators.note: precedes says the word he comes first, before the other piece

parts.note: read as mis-deed, the word deed with its letters misplaced

explanation.surface: A man is seen just before he commits some wrongdoing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'misdeed' is read as two parts: MIS, meaning wrongly placed, acting on DEED. 'precedes' puts the pronoun first.
explanation.definitionFit: To heed a warning or rule is to take notice of it and observe it.

clue.text: Reputedly happy spirit brought forth by one?

definitions.text: Reputedly happy spirit brought forth by one?

parts.words: Reputedly happy spirit brought forth by one?
parts.note: a stock phrase pairs happy with this word for a middle course, and a spiritualist of this kind summons spirits at a seance

explanation.walkthrough: Two ideas: the stock phrase 'a happy medium', and the seance where a medium calls up a spirit.
explanation.definitionFit: A medium is a person who claims to contact spirits of the dead, and 'happy medium' is a sensible middle course.

clue.text: A rather retiring circle in California?

parts.note: someone rather retiring is modest, unassuming
a circle is shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: A shy social set somewhere on the West Coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Modesto is a city in California's Central Valley, so it is one place found there.

clue.text: The train was in Patience.

parts.note: in Gilbert and Sullivan's opera Patience the lovesick maidens sing that they walk two and two in a mournful train

explanation.walkthrough: 'Patience' reads as calm endurance, but it is the Gilbert and Sullivan operetta, where the maidens' procession is a doleful train.
explanation.definitionFit: Doleful means mournful and sorrowful, the mood of the pining maidens in that opening chorus.

clue.text: Jane of Hull House.

parts.note: the social reformer who founded Hull House, the Chicago settlement house, in 1889

explanation.walkthrough: A general-knowledge clue: Hull House was the Chicago settlement house founded by the social reformer Jane Addams.
explanation.definitionFit: Addams was the surname of the Nobel Peace Prize winner who founded that Chicago social settlement.

clue.text: Where to find the point of etching to be à la mode.

definitions.text: Where to find the point of etching
definitions.meaning: first meaning, read as two words: the point of an etching tool is in the style, or stylus

explanation.walkthrough: A style is a pointed engraving tool, so its tip is literally in the style.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done in style is fashionable, which is what the French phrase means.

clue.text: See 2
Led back with the sort of dude that's easily tricked.

indicators.note: with says one piece is joined straight onto the other
back means the word led is read in the other direction
sort of means a version of the word dude with its letters shuffled

explanation.surface: A gullible city slicker from the ranch is led back to town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns LED into DEL; 'with' joins it to the next piece; 'sort of' shuffles DUDE into UDED.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone deluded has been misled, fooled into holding a false belief.

clue.text: Changes the title, perhaps.

parts.note: renaming is the surface reading, but a title is legal ownership, which is passed to someone else

explanation.walkthrough: 'Changes the title' suggests renaming a book; it means handing over a property title.
explanation.definitionFit: To transfer a deed or title is to convey ownership of property from one person to another.

clue.text: See 7 down
The part of the skimobile that's used to travel on snow.

definitions.text: that's used to travel on snow

indicators.note: part of says the answer is a portion of the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run from the last of the into the start of skimobile

explanation.surface: Which component of a snowmobile actually carries it over the snow?
explanation.definitionFit: An Eskimo is an Arctic person, someone at home travelling across snow and ice.

clue.text: Lies cold when taken apart, but ultimately comes together.

indicators.note: taken apart means broken up, so the letters of 'lies cold' are rearranged

explanation.surface: Something left cold in pieces is reassembled in the end.
explanation.definitionFit: To collide is to come together forcefully, as two cars meeting in a crash.
